intro_en:
A relatively long segment of the Israel National Trail that passes through two unique canyons: Vardit and Barak. The route then continues along one of the widest and longest streams in the country – Nahal Paran.

 Tzukim – Nahal Barak (47)
 Nahal Tzihor – Shizafon Junction (49)
character_en: Most of the route is on dirt roads that are comfortable to walk. The passage through the two canyons is with the aid of ladders, handholds and ropes. Crossing rock pools (gevim) full of water may be required. Passing through the two canyons is not compulsory, and both have bypasses.
shortcuts_en: The segment can be shortened at several points; see details under "Important to know".
pois_en: Barak Canyon. Ramat Barak. Vardit Canyon. Nahal Paran and Nahal Tzihor.
important_en: To purchase the Israel National Trail map binder, in excellent print quality and in a convenient, lightweight package
Israel National Trail guide for the Negev (segments 37-56)
The Israel National Trail main page
Recommended lodging in the area: Hatzeva Field School
Access to the overnight campsite in Nahal Barak is suitable for any vehicle. There is no water at the overnight campsite.
The segment is relatively long; it is recommended to start walking early in the morning.

The route can be shortened by starting the walk west of the Nahal Barak overnight campsite. The access into Nahal Barak is suitable for any vehicle, but only as far as the point where the road deteriorates, and that location changes.

There are two further options for shortening the segment, both accessible by 4x4 vehicle: 1. Ending at the day campsite at the exit from Vardit Canyon. 2. Ending at the overnight campsite at the confluence of Nahal Paran and Nahal Tzihor.
In some winters the rock pools in the canyons are full of water, and there is the option of bypassing both canyons.
There are no sources of drinking water along the entire route, until Tzihor Junction.
Close to the end point, across Road 40, there is an overnight campsite. The campsite has no water source.
description_en:
We set out from the Nahal Barak overnight campsite, which lies 1.5 km west of the Arava road.
We turn left towards the south-west on a blue-marked dirt road. We walk along the wide channel of Nahal Barak on the way to the Nahal Barak canyon. On our way we pass two road junctions, and the Israel National Trail continues straight through both of them together with the blue marking.
Along the way, the wide stream narrows and the walls on either side of the channel draw closer together. More acacia trees appear beside the channel as we approach the mouth of the canyon. Climbing on the acacias is a plant with red flowers and broad leaves – the acacia strap flower (Plicosepalus acaciae).
The strap flower is no "innocent" climber; it uses the tree not only as a climbing wall but also as a host. The parasitic strap flower pushes its roots into the tree's branches and draws water and minerals from them. Even so, the strap flower does see to some of its own needs – the process of photosynthesis that supplies it with sugars. Evidence of this is its broad, green, elliptical leaves. The ripe fruit is red, and inside it is a seed coated in a sticky substance. The glue lets the seed cling to the branches of the tree into which its roots will sprout. Birds, chiefly the sunbird, help disperse the seeds, which stick to their beak or foot or pass through the bird's digestive system.
Near the mouth of the Nahal Barak canyon we pass a marked trail junction at the foot of a pale step in the left wall of the channel, at the point where vehicle access into the channel is blocked. The green trail climbing to the left is a bypass of the canyon that links up with the continuation of the Israel National Trail. It climbs to the top of the canyon wall and there meets the Israel National Trail and the blue marking after the exit from the canyon.
The passage through the canyon involves climbing ladders, using ropes and sometimes swimming. We continue with the channel to the gate of the canyon, and the walls close in to a distance of just a few metres. We advance to the climb up the dry waterfalls and rock steps with the aid of ropes and ladders. Between the waterfalls there are rock pools, which fill up in the floods that pass through the stream. A glance upwards reveals the narrow, beautiful strip of sky between the canyon walls.
At the end of the short canyon, the trail turns sharply left, comes out above the gorge and walks along its rim – so that we can see the gorge from above. After a short walk, there is a meeting with the green-marked trail arriving from the left, which is walked by those who preferred to bypass the canyon.
We continue south to the expanses of Ramat Barak. On the way to Vardit Canyon, the Israel National Trail alternately follows a red-marked jeep track and, in short stretches, "cuts" the bends of the red jeep track and shortens the walk along blue-marked footpaths.
At one of the transitions from a blue footpath to the red jeep track, there are a few acacia trees in a channel. This is an opportunity to stop and rest in the shade of one of them.
On the next stretch, we should look out for a fine viewpoint to the south-east towards the Hidud Cliffs (Matzukei Hidud) and Nahal Paran.
A few minutes' walk after the acacia trees, at the point where the footpath crosses the jeep track, we reach a trail fork. A green-marked trail descends to the left – offering a bypass of Vardit Canyon. Those choosing the bypass walk the green-marked trail down a short descent and then rejoin the Israel National Trail after it exits the canyon.
Those who choose to pass through the beautiful, impressive canyon, where the gorge walls soar to a height of several tens of metres, will follow a route that includes ladders and ropes, and crossing rock pools full of water may also be required. We climb to the canyon entrance with the Israel National Trail and the blue marking. We cross a low ridge line and descend its other side into the channel of Nahal Vardit. The descent through the canyon is challenging and includes six dry waterfalls.
On exiting the canyon we meet the green trail walked by those who bypassed the canyon. The channel of Nahal Vardit widens and after a short distance passes a parking spot for 4x4 vehicles.
From the parking spot we continue along the jeep track to the wide channel of Nahal Paran. On the right stands the cliff wall of the Hidud Cliffs, the line of cliffs between the channel of Nahal Paran and Ramat Barak. We walk about 5 km along the channel of Nahal Paran.
The Paran is the longest ephemeral stream in the country. Its drainage basin, which is arc-shaped, spreads over a vast area of almost 4,000 square km, half of which lies across the border with Egypt. The general direction of the main channel is from east to west. Beyond the border with Egypt, the stream's channel continues in a long fan southwards, whose head is about 20 km west of Taba. At its southern source, the Paran shares a watershed with short streams that flow into the Gulf of Eilat, within Sinai. The northern boundary of the drainage basin reaches the rim of Makhtesh Ramon, between Mount Oded and Ma'ale Arod on the western side of Makhtesh Ramon.
The volumes of water that pass through it are enormous: in a flood in the winter of 2004 the discharge reached 1,280 cubic metres per second. For comparison, the average discharge of the upper Jordan River is 16 cubic metres per second. Its Arabic name is Wadi Jirafi, meaning "the Sweeper", and it received its Hebrew name after the biblical name – the dwelling place of Ishmael and a station in the wanderings of the Children of Israel in the desert.
The Israel National Trail follows a track hugging the southern bank of the stream. At the meeting with Nahal Tzihor, a tributary of Nahal Paran arriving from the south, the trail leaves Nahal Paran and turns south into the Tzihor.
Beside the confluence there is a designated overnight campsite, a possible end point for those equipped for it. It is important to know that there is no water source at the campsite. A black-marked road continues from here westwards to Road 40 in the Mishor area, a distance of about 7 km.
The Israel National Trail turns south along the channel of Nahal Tzihor, and continues with a blue-marked road for about 5 km, as far as Road 40 west of Tzihor Junction.
Across Road 40, beside a red-marked road leading off the highway to the south-west, there is a designated overnight campsite (the campsite has no water source).
author_en: Itzik Ben Dov, Trail Marking Coordinator, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel (SPNI).
